title: Book 3: Cremona, the Capitol and the Fall of Vitellius
sum: Book 3 is the Flavianist conquest of Italy in the autumn of AD 69. The generals of the Danube armies, led by Primus Antonius, invade, Caecina's Vitellianist army breaks apart in treason, and the Flavianists win a night battle near Cremona. They then storm the camp and sack the city. Vitellius, in Rome, hides the news, then gives up the throne in the Forum and is pulled back to the Palace. His general Fabius Valens is captured, Italy goes over to Vespasian, and the war ends in Rome itself.

In the last third of the book, Flavius Sabinus seizes the Capitol, the Vitellianists attack it, and Rome's greatest temple burns (3:71-72). Sabinus is killed, Domitian escapes in disguise, and Vitellius is dragged to the Gemonian stairs and killed. Domitian is hailed as Caesar in the last line. The Bible is never named in this book, but its world is: Syria and Egypt, Puteoli and Pontus, centurions and tribunes, omens, taxes and the emperor's name.
readings: The book is a campaign narrative: dates, marches, the second battle at Bedriacum, the assault on a camp and a city, and a final street fight. Antonius is the general of the story; Mucianus is the one who comes late. Read this way, the book is a study in what happens when armies, not the Senate, decide who rules.

Tacitus judges as he narrates. He praises Antonius in action and blames him for the sack of Cremona (3:32) and the grab for power afterward (3:49); he allows Vitellius frankness and generosity but says the army's love came through his laziness (3:86); and he says the burning of the Capitol is the saddest and most shameful thing to happen to Rome since its founding (3:72).

views.C: A Christian reader meets the Bible's world on every page: Syria and Egypt, centurions and tribunes, the title Caesar, omens, taxes, Puteoli where Paul landed, and the emperor Claudius of Acts. Here two kinds of temple stand side by side. Rome's greatest temple burns by the hands of Romans (3:71), and the next year the Jerusalem temple falls to Roman soldiers, which many readers connect with Jesus' words (Mark 13:2). The Bible is never named in this book, and it never mentions Jews or Christians. The measure the site uses is the Bible's. Paul wrote to Christians in Rome, "There is no authority that does not come from God" (Romans 13:1), and Peter and the apostles said, "Obeying God has to come before obeying people" (Acts 5:29); the topic page on church and state sets out how the traditions weigh the two. The ruler who "does not carry the sword for no reason" (Romans 13:4) is, in Tacitus, a man who offers his dagger to a consul as he steps down (3:68).
views.H: Tacitus wrote about AD 100 to 110, a generation after the events (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). He names some of his sources in this book: Vipstanus Messalla, a tribune in the Flavianist army (3:9, 3:25, 3:28), and Gaius Plinius (3:28), and he names Cluvius Rufus and Silius Italicus as the two witnesses to a meeting (3:65). Wikipedia's article on the year says some scholars argue that the new regime distorted the events, especially through the writings of the historian Tacitus; the scholars behind that claim are not named here. The other ancient accounts agree on the outline and differ on details such as who lit the Capitol (3:71) and Vitellius's age (3:86). The Wikipedia article on the second battle of Bedriacum lists Greenhalgh (1975), Dupuy and Dupuy (1986) and Grant (1975) among its modern sources for the campaign.
views.R: The Roman world is on every page: the legions and their numbers, auxiliary cavalry wings, the Praetorian cohorts and their prefects, the city cohorts and the night watch (3:64), the consul with his lictors (3:31), the praetor and the sacred right of envoys (3:80), the Vestal Virgins (3:81), the omens and sacrifices (3:56), the oath to the emperor (3:13), the Capitol and the temples of Jupiter, and the Saturnalia (3:78). Tacitus also shows how the empire was held together by colonies like Cremona, by client kings like Sido and Italicus, and by the emperor's freedmen such as Hormus (3:12).
views.J: Josephus tells the same year from the East: Vespasian declared emperor, Mucianus, Alexandria's grain, Antonius and the sack of Cremona, Sabinus on the Capitol, the temple burned, Domitian's escape, and Vitellius's death, then Titus sent to Jerusalem (War 4.601-658). Suetonius adds the rumor that men from Judea would rule the world (Vespasian 4.5). Josephus (Antiquities 20.139-146) shows Berenice marrying Polemon of Cilicia, linked to Tacitus's Polemon at 3:47. Acts gives the Roman officers and Roman places of the same decades. The Gospels and Acts say nothing of the year 69 itself.

deep.b: Tacitus runs the book in four moves. Chapters 1-9 tell how the Flavianist generals chose to march, took the north of Italy and faced Caecina's camp, where the commander was already settling the terms of his treason. Chapters 10-18 tell the mutinies, Caecina's betrayal and the first fighting near Cremona. Chapters 19-35 tell the night battle, the storming of the camp and the sack of Cremona. Chapters 36-86 tell, side by side, Vitellius's decline in Rome and the Flavianist advance down to Rome, ending in the fire on the Capitol, the street fighting and the death of Vitellius. The dates Tacitus gives are few: Rosius Regulus's one-day consulship on 31 October (3:37) and Vitellius's surrender on 18 December (3:67). The battle at Cremona was on 24 October 69 and Vitellius's death on 20 December (Wikipedia).

deep.h: How the other ancient writers tell it
deep.b: Josephus (War 4) tells the same end with his own focus: Vespasian made emperor by his men, Mucianus, Alexandria and the grain, the clash on the Capitol, Domitian's escape and Vitellius's death, and then Titus sent to Jerusalem (4.601-658). He also tells Cremona, in a much shorter and different form (War 4.11.2-3, in Whiston's numbering): Caecina's army deserts to Antonius, repents the same night and puts Caecina in bonds; Antonius beats the revolters, takes Cremona and "gave leave to his soldiers to plunder it." Josephus counts 30,200 dead of Vitellius's army and 4,500 of Antonius's men. Those figures are Josephus's own and are not checked against anything else. Tacitus has 40,000 armed men burst into the town (3:33), says Antonius spoke of the victors and the beaten and "said nothing either way about Cremona" (3:32), and has him forbid keeping Cremonans as captives only after the sack (3:34). Suetonius gives the Capitol fire, Vitellius's death and age, and Domitian's disguise as an Isis follower. Cassius Dio, in the later Epitome, has Antonius, the Capitol fire and the end of Vitellius, but gives his age as 54 years and 89 days; in its account of the city taken after the night battle (64.15) the gates are opened, "all the soldiers were granted leave," and fifty thousand die in all, counting those killed in the battle. Plutarch mentions the Capitol's burning only in passing (Publicola 15). They all agree on the shape of the story. They differ on who lit the Capitol and on details of how Vitellius died; see the notes at 3:71, 3:84 and 3:86.

Where Book 3 touches the Bible

Every person, place, event, office and custom in this book that the Bible (or Josephus on the Bible's world) also names. "Strong" means the same person, place or event; "background" means the same world only.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a pair of fires
deep.b:
Claude's own theory, labeled as such. Tacitus mourns the Capitol (3:72) in a book that never mentions Jews or Christians. He calls the burning "the saddest and most shameful" thing to happen to Rome since its founding. The Jerusalem temple burned the next year (Josephus, War 6.4.5), and Jesus had said of that temple that "not one stone will be left on a stone" (Mark 13:2). A Jewish or Christian reader meeting Tacitus's lament over Rome's temple could set the two losses side by side. The two fires, however, were set by opposite sides of the same civil-war year: Josephus has the soldiers "that came from Germany" for Vitellius take the Capitol hill and burn the temple (War 4.649), while Vespasian's side, which won, sent Titus from Alexandria to Jerusalem with "a select part of his army" (War 4.658). Tacitus gives a different ancient reading of the Capitol fire: the Gauls took it as a sign that Rome's rule was ending, and the Druids called it a sign of heaven's anger (4:54).

Overlap with scholarship: one general web search for scholars who set the Capitol fire of AD 69 beside the temple fire of AD 70 turned up popular histories and Wikipedia's pages on Josephus and the siege, none that sets the two fires side by side. The idea may still be in print elsewhere; this page does not claim it is new.

settings.what: The council of war at Petovio
settings.by: The Flavianist leaders, with the voices for waiting set out first
settings.to: The Flavianist generals and commanders
settings.when: In the winter camp of the 13th legion, at the start of the campaign
settings.why: To decide whether to hold the Alpine passes until Mucianus and the East arrived or to strike at once into Italy. Tacitus gives the case for waiting before the case for speed, so the reader weighs both before Antonius speaks.
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Antonius's speech for striking at once
settings.to: The council, with centurions and some common soldiers pushing in to hear
settings.when: At the council of war at Petovio
settings.why: To win the plan of invading Italy before the Vitellianists recovered. He argues that the Vitellianist soldiers have gone soft in Italy, that their reinforcements are near, and that the Flavianist cavalry was not beaten. The speech also made him the soldiers' favorite, and Tacitus says it won over even the cautious (3:3).
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Vespasian's order to halt at Aquileia, and Mucianus's letters
settings.by: Vespasian, by order; Mucianus, in frequent letters
settings.to: The Flavianist generals in northern Italy
settings.when: After the generals had taken Vicetia and Verona and blocked the German route, moves Tacitus says were made either without Vespasian's knowledge or against his orders
settings.why: To hold the army until Mucianus arrived. Vespasian's argument was that, holding Egypt, which controls the grain supply, and the revenues of the richest provinces, he could force Vitellius's army to give up for lack of pay and food. Mucianus's letters said the same and offered "a victory that would cost neither blood nor tears," but Tacitus says he was really greedy for glory and wanted the credit for the war. Because of the distances, "the advice always arrived after the matter was settled."
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Caecina's letter to the Flavianist legions, and the leaders' replies
settings.by: Caecina, by letter; the Flavianist leaders, in reply
settings.to: The Flavianist legions, with the 7th just arrived under Aponius Saturninus; then the Vitellianist tribunes and centurions, and Caecina himself
settings.when: While Caecina's camp stood between Hostilia and the marshes of the Tartarus, before the Moesian army had joined the Flavianists
settings.why: Caecina's letter blamed the Flavianists for "recklessly taking up arms again for a beaten cause" and praised the German army's courage. He mentioned Vitellius only briefly and said nothing against Vespasian, so that, in Tacitus's words, "he said nothing that could either win over or frighten the enemy." Tacitus says Caecina kept wasting time and scolding in letters "until his envoys had settled the terms of his treason." The leaders' replies praised Vespasian, held out to the tribunes and centurions the hope of keeping the privileges Vitellius had granted them, and urged Caecina himself to change sides. Read out before the assembled army, the letters raised its confidence, because Caecina had written humbly and the Flavianist leaders scornfully.
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Antonius quiets the mutiny and prays to the standards
settings.to: The mutinous legions at Verona, then the standards and "the gods of war"
settings.when: When the soldiers turned on Flavianus and would not hear their own officers
settings.why: To stop the soldiers murdering their legate and to turn the army's anger away from its own side. His prayer asks that the madness and infighting go to the enemy's armies. It is a rare prayer in this book: Tacitus gives its content but no answer from the gods.
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Vespasian's letter to Flavianus
settings.to: Tampius Flavianus
settings.when: On the road, when Flavianus left the camp at Verona the night the mutiny wore itself out
settings.why: To get Flavianus out of danger. Tacitus gives no words of it, only that it "met him on the way and got him out of danger."
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Caecina's address and the soldiers' outcry
settings.by: Caecina to the chief centurions; then the Vitellianist soldiers
settings.to: First a few chief centurions and soldiers at headquarters; then the whole German army
settings.when: On learning that the Ravenna fleet had gone over
settings.why: Caecina wants to carry the army over to Vespasian by an oath. The soldiers' cry tells him what he did not expect: that they will not be handed over without a fight, "like a herd of slaves for sale." The reader learns that the treason was Caecina's and the generals', not the army's.
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Antonius holds the army back from Cremona
settings.to: The Flavianist soldiers, standing at night before Cremona
settings.when: At evening after the cavalry battle, when the soldiers shouted to march on Cremona at once
settings.why: To keep the army from a night assault with no scouting, no ladders and no engines. He argues that the general's part is foresight and the soldier's part is courage. Tacitus lets the reader see the soldiers' real thought first: plunder goes to the army that storms, not to the one that waits.
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Antonius's appeals to the legions at night in the battle
settings.to: The Pannonian legions, the Moesian troops, the 3rd legion and the Praetorians in turn
settings.when: In the last hours of the night battle outside Cremona, when the line wavered
settings.why: To stir each body of men with its own shame or its own glory. He reminds the Pannonians of their earlier defeat, the Moesians that they began the war, and the 3rd of its victories over the Parthians, Armenians and Sarmatae. He calls the Praetorians "civilians" and tells them defeat is death.
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: The dying father and the son
settings.by: A Flavianist soldier (Tacitus has the story from Vipstanus Messalla)
settings.to: The father he has just struck down, who was fighting on the Vitellianist side
settings.when: On the road to Cremona, at the end of the night battle
settings.why: To ask pardon and to say that the guilt is shared by all. It is there to show what civil war does to a family. Tacitus says he gives names on Messalla's authority.
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Antonius's assembly after the surrender
settings.to: The Flavianist soldiers at Cremona
settings.when: Just after the Vitellianists had given up and the people of Cremona were being roughly handled
settings.why: Antonius praised the victors and spoke kindly to the beaten, and said nothing either way about Cremona. By staying silent he let the army's old hatred take its course. Tacitus does not quote the words; he reports what was left out.
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Vitellius's praise of the soldiers, and his speech to the Senate
settings.to: A crowded assembly in Rome; then the Senate
settings.when: When he came back to the city after learning that Caecina had revolted and the army had put him in chains (3:36); then in the Senate (3:37)
settings.why: Tacitus gives no words of either. He shows their effects: joy over the soldiers' loyalty, and in the Senate a speech "composed for grandeur" that the senators answered with studied flattery, with the first savage motion against Caecina coming from Lucius Vitellius. Tacitus has just said that Vitellius "made no preparations for war."
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Lucius Vitellius accuses Junius Blaesus
settings.to: His brother, the emperor Vitellius, who was ill
settings.when: In the emperor's bedroom, when Vitellius had seen a tower lit by lamps across the garden
settings.why: To turn the emperor's annoyance into a death sentence for Blaesus, who was a rival in birth and reputation. Lucius says the enemy to guard against is not Vespasian but a man in Rome with imperial ancestors. Tacitus says Lucius hated Blaesus out of rivalry, so the reader hears a motive behind the warning.

settings.what: Valens's letter to Vitellius
settings.to: Vitellius
settings.when: After Valens had wasted the time for action in delay and rejected both plans (3:40)
settings.why: To ask for help. Three cohorts and a British cavalry regiment came, which Tacitus calls "too many to slip by unnoticed and too few to force a way through."
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Mucianus's letters to Primus, Varus and Plotius Griphus
settings.to: Primus Antonius and Varus; Plotius Griphus and the other men Mucianus could count on
settings.when: After Cremona, while Antonius and the other Flavianist generals were planning the advance across the Apennines
settings.why: To keep Mucianus's own chance of a share in the war's glory. To Primus and Varus he wrote in "middle-of-the-road terms" so that he could deny a failure or claim a success; to Griphus and the others he gave plainer instructions. Their replies criticized the haste of Primus and Varus, and Mucianus sent those replies on to Vespasian, so that Antonius's plans and deeds would not be valued as Antonius had hoped.
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Antonius's letter to Vespasian
settings.to: Vespasian, in Egypt
settings.when: After Cremona, when Mucianus's letters had cheapened his deeds
settings.why: To claim the credit for the Italian victory and answer Mucianus. Tacitus says the letter was "more arrogant than anyone should use to an emperor." It lists what Antonius did and says that those who were not in the danger should not win its rewards.
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Julius Agrestis's last words
settings.to: Vitellius, who had accused him of being bribed
settings.when: After Agrestis went to see the beaten army at Cremona and came back to report
settings.why: To prove his report was true when the emperor would not believe it. He said, "Since you need strong proof," and he would give something to believe. Tacitus says some reported that Vitellius had him killed, but that both versions agree on his loyalty.
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Vitellius's address to the troops at Mevania
settings.to: The army at the camp at Mevania, which had demanded him
settings.when: On his arrival at the camp, as the omens appeared
settings.why: Tacitus gives none of the words. He gives what happened while Vitellius spoke: birds hid the daylight and a bull broke from the altar (see the omen note at 3:56), and then shows a leader who "knew nothing of soldiering."
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Antonius calms the army at Carsulae
settings.to: The Flavianist soldiers, impatient for battle
settings.when: At Carsulae, with the Vitellianists ten miles away
settings.why: To keep the soldiers from rushing the enemy and from wrecking Rome. "The beginning of a civil war has to be left to luck. Victory is finished by plans and reason." Tacitus ends with "Words like these calmed their spirits."
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Offers of safety to Vitellius
settings.by: Primus Antonius and Varus, by messages; Mucianus, in letters in the same terms
settings.to: Vitellius
settings.when: After the Vitellianist soldiers went over at Narnia
settings.why: To get Vitellius to lay down his arms and put himself and his children in Vespasian's hands, in return for safety, money and a quiet retreat in Campania. Vitellius mostly trusted them and began to talk of how many slaves he would take and where on the coast he would live.
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: The leading men urge Sabinus to act
settings.to: Flavius Sabinus, prefect of the city and brother of Vespasian
settings.when: In private talks, while the Flavianist army was still north of Rome
settings.why: To make Sabinus take Rome himself, ahead of Antonius and Varus. They say Vitellius has few cohorts and that "the credit for ending the war will go to whoever takes the city."
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Vitellius's friends urge him to fight
settings.to: Vitellius in the Palace
settings.when: When Vitellius was ready to give up the throne
settings.why: To stop him from surrendering, since a defeated emperor could not be allowed to live. They end: "If we are beaten, we must die, and if we surrender, we must die." Vitellius did not listen.
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Vitellius's farewell to the people
settings.to: The crowd in the Forum, his soldiers and the watching women
settings.when: On 18 December, in his own assembly
settings.why: To say that he gave up the throne for peace and for the state, and to ask people to remember him and pity his brother, wife and children. He offered his dagger to the consul as a sign of giving back the power of life and death. The crowd refused to let him go.
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Sabinus's complaint to Vitellius
settings.by: Flavius Sabinus, by the messenger Cornelius Martialis
settings.to: Vitellius in the Palace
settings.when: At dawn on the day after Sabinus took the Capitol, before blows had been struck
settings.why: To say that the agreement had been broken: Vitellius had gone back to the Palatine and sent an armed column out. Sabinus asks him to meet the legions in the field and leave an old man and a boy alone. Vitellius answered, helpless, that the soldiers would not obey him.
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: The secret letters said to come from Vitellius to Antonius
settings.to: Primus Antonius
settings.when: While the Flavianist army spent the holiday days of Saturn idle at Ocriculum
settings.why: The charge was that Vitellius had offered a consulship, a marriageable daughter and a rich dowry as the price of betrayal, and that this explained Antonius's delay. Tacitus gives the story with two other explanations of the delay and does not choose between them.
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.
views: Some accused Antonius of delaying treacherously after secret letters from Vitellius offering a consulship, a marriageable daughter and a rich dowry as the price of betrayal.
A story made up to please Mucianus
Others said the story was made up to please Mucianus.
A plan to show the war to the city
Some said the plan of all the generals was to show the war to the city rather than bring it, since the strongest cohorts had deserted Vitellius and he seemed likely to give up the throne.

settings.what: Musonius Rufus's lecture and the Vestals' letter
settings.by: Musonius Rufus; the Vestal Virgins with a letter from Vitellius
settings.to: The armed soldiers at the gates of Rome; Antonius
settings.when: As the Senate's envoys reached the Flavianist army
settings.why: The Stoic spoke on the blessings of peace and the soldiers laughed. The Vestals brought Vitellius's request for one day's delay; Antonius sent them away with honor and replied that the death of Sabinus and the burning of the Capitol had "ended all dealings of war."
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: Antonius's assembly of the legions at the Mulvian Bridge
settings.to: The Flavianist legions
settings.when: As the army came up to Rome
settings.why: To make the legions camp near the Mulvian Bridge and enter the city the next day, because he feared that soldiers worked up by the fighting would show no regard for the people, the Senate or the temples and shrines of the gods. The soldiers saw any postponement as hostile to victory.
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

settings.what: The soldiers' cry at the camp, and Vitellius's last words
settings.to: Each other and the Vitellianists in the camp; then a tribune who was insulting Vitellius
settings.when: During the storming of the camp, then in the Forum before the Gemonian stairs
settings.why: The soldiers said that they had returned the city to the Senate and the temples to the gods, but that "a soldier's honor is in his camp." Vitellius, when insulted, answered, "Yet I was your emperor."
settings.readers: Roman readers a generation after the events, around AD 100 to 110 (Wikipedia's article on the Histories). Tacitus writes of "our ancestors" and "the Roman people" (3:72), so he counts on readers who know Rome's story and its families.

traditions.q: May a Christian serve as a soldier or take part in a war?
views: Yes, under strict conditions. The Catechism lists four that must hold "at one and the same time": the damage "must be lasting, grave, and certain"; "all other means ... must have been shown to be impractical or ineffective"; "there must be serious prospects of success"; and "the use of arms must not produce evils and disorders graver than the evil to be eliminated" (Catechism 2309). It also says authorities "should make equitable provision for those who for reasons of conscience refuse to bear arms" (Catechism 2311).

Yes. The Augsburg Confession (Article XVI) teaches that "it is right for Christians to bear civil office, to sit as judges ... to engage in just wars, to serve as soldiers," and condemns the Anabaptists who forbid these offices to Christians.

Yes. The Westminster Confession (chapter 23, section 2) says "It is lawful for Christians to accept and execute the office of a magistrate, when called thereunto," and that for the sake of piety, justice and peace "they may lawfully, now under the new testament, wage war, upon just and necessary occasion."

No. The Schleitheim Confession (Article VI, in J. C. Wenger's translation) says "The sword is ordained of God outside the perfection of Christ. It punishes and puts to death the wicked, and guards and protects the good," and that the worldly magistrates use it, while among the Christians "only the ban is used for a warning and for the excommunication of the one who has sinned." It adds that "it is not appropriate for a Christian to serve as a magistrate," because the magistrates' weapons are carnal "but the Christians' weapons are spiritual, against the fortification of the devil."

No. The 1660 Declaration to the king says that "the Spirit of Christ, which leads us into all truth, will never move us to fight and war against any man with outward weapons, neither for the kingdom of Christ, nor for the kingdoms of this world."
